trial.ground_truth: Five immediate retries per failed payment call without backoff
trial.predicted_root_cause: payment-service /charge returns 503 on ~99.7% of requests in 2.8–4ms, i.e. a fast-fail before meaningful downstream I/O. Two independent sources corroborate: (1) sampled logs contain only payment-service /charge 503 ERROR groups (two 60-row samples, no other error-producing service), and (2) trace cf3813d839d20d97ce0e84da4a3a79f1 shows the causal chain gateway 502 -> order-service /checkout 502 -> order-service POST 503 -> payment-service POST /charge 503, while the payment-service child span EXISTS (redis) succeeds in 0.457ms with error=false. Database state is idle: all pg_stat_activity sessions (including payment-service) are idle in ClientRead, and pg_stat_statements call_deltas are all 0 with sub-ms mean exec times (pg_sleep test query excluded), so Postgres is not the bottleneck. Redis counters are cumulative hits/misses with no error component. Because a 503 is produced in milliseconds with healthy cache and DB dependencies, the fault is inside payment-service's charge path (error branch/exception/configuration of its own logic or payment-provider dependency), not a slow downstream. order-service's ~4.9x repeated /charge calls (5 calls, ~14–18ms intervals, request_ratio 4.95) amplify the load but do not originate the errors; gateway errors are pure propagation. NOTE: the exact error branch was not confirmed — the charge-handler source was not readable within the allowed scope (search_repository located references only; get_code_symbol/get_code_context not available/insufficient), so the precise internal trigger remains unverified and the deepest root cause is UNKNOWN.

regression_risks: Recommended retry/backoff reduction on order-service may mask the failure rather than fix it, and could change latency/error SLOs if the true cause is a transient dependency that still needs retries.

With no code patch applied and no deployed change tied to the incident, the fault may recur; operational steps (env/flag inspection, rollback) could alter unrelated behavior if applied without a confirmed revision diff.
Adding a 503 error-branch metric/log tag changes telemetry only, but if done incorrectly could inflate error cardinality or mis-tag dependency failures as internal fast-fails.
critic_result.test_sufficiency: Insufficient. No code location, 503 body/error code, config/revision snapshot, or before/after controlled test is provided. Recovery (E-7447b7d698b34392) is an observational before/after with no isolated intervention, and the claimed 2.8-4ms fast-fail conflicts with 7.8-13.8ms /charge spans in the trace. Root cause remains unverified as the diagnosis itself states.
critic_result.verification_summary:
Localization (payment-service /charge is the deepest observed failing span) is well supported. Trace cf3813d839... (E-c6d5b5cf77804c0b, E-8d843b0d633d4f44) shows gateway 502 -> order-service /checkout 502 -> order-service POST 503 -> payment-service POST /charge 503, with the only observed child (redis EXISTS, 0.457ms, error=false) succeeding; sampled logs (E-b3c1fa4be8674672, E-0e01ed920aff4aab, E-51c3e143b5df4a74) contain only payment /charge 503 and order /checkout 502 groups. Metrics (E-429c4577e3bb42c4) show payment 100% error at 3.41ms avg, consistent with fast-fail.

However the diagnosis labels its own deepest root cause UNKNOWN and no code location was read, so the claimed mechanism ("internal error branch before downstream I/O") is an inference, not evidence. The trace shows /charge spans lasting 7.8-13.8ms, NOT the 2.8-4ms asserted; the 3.41-6.15ms figures come from aggregate per-service HTTP metrics, which may measure a different span boundary. This weakens the "no downstream I/O" timing argument. No 503 body/message, error code, or config snapshot is in evidence. Critically, E-429c4577e3bb42c4 shows the failure surfaced as near-simultaneous onset of 100% errors with throughput collapse in order/notification, and E-7447b7d698b34392 shows full recovery to 0% errors with request counts dropping 360->76, i.e. the anomaly may correlate with the load generator / retry amplification rather than a config change; the 4.95x retry ratio could itself be the trigger for an overload-induced fast 503. A NO_CODE_PATCH operational diagnosis is reasonable, but the origin conclusion is not independently confirmed.

alternative_explanations: Self-inflicted load/retry amplification: order-service's 4.95x retries (360 vs 76 requests) may overload payment-service, producing fast 503s; error onset and recovery track load, not a config change. Payment fast-fail could be a local circuit-breaker/rate-limit rejecting excess traffic.

Payment-provider or downstream gRPC/HTTP dependency failure not captured as a child span: an un-instrumented outbound call could return immediately (connection refused/instant 503 from a sidecar/service mesh), which would look like an internal fast-fail without a visible failing child span.

Non-deterministic/environmental cause (e.g., payment pod restart, credential expiry, or a bad revision) that coincidentally resolved; no deployment/config/revision evidence is present to distinguish this from an in-handler error branch.

judgment.explanation: The diagnosis correctly identifies the amplification mechanism (order-service issuing ~5 repeated /charge calls, ratio ~4.95, at ~15ms spacing) and correctly notes the fast-fail 503s and propagation, but it attributes the origin to payment-service /charge returning 503 on ~99.7% of requests, i.e. a payment-service internal fast-fail. Ground truth is a Retry Storm in order-service: immediate retries per failed call without backoff, amplified by a failing payment call. The affected/originating service is order-service's retry policy, not an internal payment defect. The diagnosis inverts origin and amplification—it treats order-service retries as mere 'amplification' and payment /charge as the origin—so the causal mechanism and service attribution are materially wrong. It also labels the deepest root cause UNKNOWN rather than the retry storm. Evidence quality is 2: independent supporting observations (trace chain, log groups, retry ratio metrics).

However the diagnosis labels its own deepest root cause UNKNOWN and no code location was read, so the claimed mechanism ("internal error branch before downstream I/O") is an inference, not evidence. The trace shows /charge spans lasting 7.8-13.8ms, NOT the 2.8-4ms asserted; the 3.41-6.15ms figures come from aggregate per-service HTTP metrics, which may measure a different span boundary. This weakens the "no downstream I/O" timing argument. No 503 body/message, error code, or config snapshot is in evidence. decision.hypothesis: payment-service /charge is the origin of the failure chain: it fails fast (2.8–4ms, 503) on 99.7% of requests, before/without any downstream I/O (Redis EXISTS child span succeeds in 0.457ms with no error; Postgres sessions all idle in ClientRead with zero call deltas), so the 503 is generated inside the /charge handler path rather than by a slow downstream. order-service /checkout (502/503, ~98.6% errors) and gateway (502, ~50%) are propagation, with order-service's ~4.9x retry ratio against /charge amplifying load.
decision.root_cause: payment-service /charge returns 503 on ~99.7% of requests in 2.8–4ms, i.e. a fast-fail before meaningful downstream I/O. Two independent sources corroborate: (1) sampled logs contain only payment-service /charge 503 ERROR groups (two 60-row samples, no other error-producing service), and (2) trace cf3813d839d20d97ce0e84da4a3a79f1 shows the causal chain gateway 502 -> order-service /checkout 502 -> order-service POST 503 -> payment-service POST /charge 503, while the payment-service child span EXISTS (redis) succeeds in 0.457ms with error=false. Database state is idle: all pg_stat_activity sessions (including payment-service) are idle in ClientRead, and pg_stat_statements call_deltas are all 0 with sub-ms mean exec times (pg_sleep test query excluded), so Postgres is not the bottleneck. Redis counters are cumulative hits/misses with no error component. Because a 503 is produced in milliseconds with healthy cache and DB dependencies, the fault is inside payment-service's charge path (error branch/exception/configuration of its own logic or payment-provider dependency), not a slow downstream. order-service's ~4.9x repeated /charge calls (5 calls, ~14–18ms intervals, request_ratio 4.95) amplify the load but do not originate the errors; gateway errors are pure propagation. NOTE: the exact error branch was not confirmed — the charge-handler source was not readable within the allowed scope (search_repository located references only; get_code_symbol/get_code_context not available/insufficient), so the precise internal trigger remains unverified and the deepest root cause is UNKNOWN.
llm_findings: Trace causality: every upstream error span is a parent of the payment-service POST /charge 503 span; the only payment child span (redis EXISTS) succeeds, so payment-service is the deepest observed failing component.

payment-service fails in 2.8-4ms before any slow dependent work: Postgres sessions all idle in ClientRead with zero call deltas and sub-ms mean exec; Redis EXISTS returns in 0.457ms without error — excluding DB/pool/cache as the payment failure mechanism.
order-service's 5 repeated /charge calls (ratio 4.95, 14-18ms spacing) are the caller's retry policy amplifying load, so order-service and gateway errors are symptoms, not origins.

Cumulative Redis counters (54402 hits / 222694 misses) and pool counters are cumulative totals, not current activity; no error component is present, so they do not evidence a live cache or pool incident.
payment-service /health returns 200/healthy while /charge 503s, so the health endpoint does not exercise the charge path and cannot be used to disprove the failure.
Exact internal trigger of the /charge 503 (error branch/config) could not be confirmed because charge-handler source was not readable in scope; deepest cause left UNKNOWN.
decision.recommended_fix: Operational (no code patch applied; charge-handler source outside readable scope): (1) Inspect payment-service /charge handler and its deployment config for the error branch producing an immediate 503 — check required env vars/feature flags, payment-provider credentials/URL, and any fail-fast guard (e.g. an unset key or disabled provider) that short-circuits before the redis/DB calls. (2) Compare the currently deployed payment-service revision/env against the last known-good revision; roll back or restore the missing configuration. (3) Reduce order-service's retry ratio/backoff against /charge (5 attempts at ~15ms spacing, ratio 4.95) to stop amplifying load once payment recovers. (4) Add an explicit metric/log tag on the /charge 503 error branch (distinct from dependency failures) so fast-fail internal errors are directly attributable without source access.
decision.reasoning_summary: Two independent sources localize the origin to payment-service /charge: log groups showing only payment-service 503s, and the distributed trace chain in which every upstream span (gateway 502, order-service /checkout 502, order-service POST 503) is a parent of the failing payment-service POST /charge 503. The failing span's only observed child, redis EXISTS, succeeds (0.457ms, no error), and Postgres is idle (ClientRead, zero call deltas, sub-ms exec) — so downstream dependencies are healthy, ruling out DATABASE_SLOW_QUERY, DB_POOL_EXHAUSTION as the payment failure, and CACHE_MISS as a latency cause (cumulative hit/miss counters with no error, low-latency fast-fail). The 2.8–4ms fast-fail with 99.7% error rate is inconsistent with DOWNSTREAM_TIMEOUT (no I/O wait) and consistent with an internal error branch in /charge. order-service's 4.9x repeated identical calls are the caller's retry policy, so order-service and gateway are symptoms, not origins. Because the handler source could not be read to name the exact failing branch/condition, the deepest cause is reported as UNKNOWN with a concrete next step rather than claiming an unverified internal defect.
